pages.title: Fleet and instrument management services
text: Fleet services should help a laboratory understand the condition and configuration of its instruments. A useful fleet view reports calibration validity, software versions, storage health, outstanding faults and synchronization state. It should not require central access to every patient-linked image to provide those functions.
## A proposed service model

Routine telemetry should contain the minimum information needed for instrument support. A service operator may need a fault code, configuration identifier and diagnostic trace, while the laboratory retains control of clinical records. Access to a specific image for troubleshooting should be a separate, authorized action with an audit trail.

The service can coordinate signed software packages, staged updates and rollback. Instruments in the middle of a run should retain their active qualified configuration. A fleet update should not create a mixture of rules or models within one result record.
## Contract the responsibilities

The laboratory, instrument provider and hosting provider should agree who can authorize remote actions, who responds to alerts and how incidents are escalated. Service availability targets should be negotiated against the deployment context and demonstrated operating data. This compendium does not assign a contractual uptime promise.

A fleet service becomes valuable when it reduces uncertainty about instrument readiness and recovery. A dashboard full of nominally green indicators is inadequate if it cannot reveal stale telemetry, failed checks or a disconnected instrument.

pages.title: Calibration and measurement services
text: Calibration services connect instrument output to a defined measurement basis. For an imaging reader, the central task is spatial calibration at the relevant object plane, supported by checks of field dependence, stability and configuration control. Other sensing configurations require their own reference materials, transfer functions and uncertainty budgets.
## Deliver a usable calibration record

A service report should identify the instrument and configuration, the reference used, the measured residuals, the permitted operating range and the conditions that invalidate the calibration. A coefficient file without this context is insufficient for laboratory review or later investigation.

The proposed service should also distinguish calibration from adjustment. Calibration characterizes a relationship; adjustment changes the instrument. After an adjustment, the resulting measurement performance needs to be established again. Routine checks can detect departure from an accepted state, but they should not be labelled a full calibration unless they fulfil that function. [R16]
## Make serviceability a design input

Reference targets need accessible placement, stable mounting and protection from damage. The instrument should allow a service engineer to verify the measurement plane without dismantling unrelated assemblies. Calibration effort, required expertise and replacement logistics should therefore influence the design early, rather than being treated as an after-sales detail.

pages.title: Maintenance and repair services
text: Maintenance services preserve a qualified operating state and restore it after faults. They include inspection, cleaning-compatible component care, replacement, software recovery and requalification where a change can affect measurement. The scope should be specific to the instrument configuration and the laboratory’s use conditions.
## Classify the intervention by its effect

A replacement storage device may affect data integrity and recovery. A replacement light source may affect exposure, spectral response and contrast. A camera or lens change can alter the spatial measurement chain. These interventions should not share a generic “service complete” test.
## Support recovery at the laboratory

The service offer should define how users report a fault, what information is collected, when remote diagnosis is permitted and when a physical intervention is required. Spare-part planning should consider lead time, interchangeability and the evidence needed after substitution. A replacement that fits mechanically may still change the measurement behaviour.

Maintenance records should link to instrument configuration history so that later analysis can identify observations acquired before and after a change. This also supports investigation of recurring faults. The measure of a successful service is restoration of a verified, usable function with its records intact, not simply replacement of the component that first appeared suspicious.

pages.title: Training and competency services
text: Training should enable users to recognize valid operation, uncertain evidence and situations requiring an alternative workflow. It should develop the ability to challenge the software when appropriate. Familiarity with the interface alone is not evidence of measurement or review competency.
## Build training around realistic decisions

A proposed training programme should include plate identity resolution, capture readiness, calibration status, overlay inspection, correction, rejection and export reconciliation. Difficult examples should be included deliberately: glare, unclear edges, incomplete context and disagreement between the visible image and the automated estimate.

Competency evaluation should ask users to make decisions on cases they have not already memorized. The evaluation should preserve the distinction between learning the interface and demonstrating the judgement required for the laboratory’s intended role.
## Keep training current

A substantial change in overlays, quality flags, rules interpretation or export behaviour may require targeted retraining. The change should be assessed for its effect on user decisions rather than simply whether a button moved. Training records should identify the product version and the relevant tasks.

The service can include guided demonstrations, practice cases, assessed exercises and refresher material. Claims that training reduces errors or review time should be supported by evaluation, including whether users become excessively trusting of the automated output. Human review works only when the human has the information, time and competence to perform it.

pages.title: Research and data partnership services
text: Research support services can help partners turn a broad idea into a reproducible investigation. The useful deliverable is a defined question, a suitable observation plan, a provenance-preserving dataset and an analysis that distinguishes evidence from interpretation. Scientific conclusions remain the responsibility of the investigators and their review process.
## Proposed support functions

AMReye.AI could support instrument configuration, acquisition metadata, annotation workflows, data quality review, interface development and reproducible analysis packaging. Partners may also need help comparing candidate sensing approaches against a conventional baseline before committing to a larger study.
## Agree the evidence and rights in advance

Data-sharing terms should address permitted reuse, confidentiality, publication review, attribution and handling of derived models. A partner’s access to an instrument should not imply permission to reuse identifiable records for unrelated model training. Similarly, a promising preliminary result should not become a public product claim before the relevant evidence review.

Research support should be evaluated by reproducibility and usefulness: whether another analyst can understand the dataset, reconstruct the processing and identify the limits of the conclusion. A large volume of generated analysis is not a substitute for an answer to the original research question. The service should make uncertainty explicit enough to guide the next experiment or engineering decision.
